title: Six notes hiding in the static
allegory: Fourier basis analysis is like writing a recorded chord as sheet music: the recording is a dense wiggle of samples, but the sheet says just six notes, and nothing about the sound is lost.
map: the recording: one air-pressure sample per instant
W_E in the standard basis: one row per input number 0-112
pure notes, each fitting the bar exactly
the Fourier basis: a constant plus cos and sin for k = 1..56
rewriting the chord as sheet music
F @ W_E: the same matrix re-expressed in the wave basis
six notes on the sheet, the rest silent
non-trivial norm only at the key frequencies (14, 31, 35, 41, 42, 52)
nothing about the sound lost in the rewrite
an orthonormal change of basis: a rotation that keeps every length
credit: Sound-into-pure-notes framing borrowed from 3Blue1Brown, 'But what is the Fourier Transform? A visual introduction'

cap.1: A tiny model learned to add on a 113-hour clock. Its table of numbers looks like pure static. The pattern is there; you are reading it in the wrong language.
cap.2: The model does x + y mod 113. Its embedding W_E has one row per number, and read number by number every entry looks dense and random. The fix is a change of basis.
cap.3: In the standard basis W_E is dense. The move in Nanda et al. (2023) is to re-express it in the 1D Fourier basis over the input, where it turns out to be sparse.

cap.1: A recording of a chord is a messy wiggle, sample after sample. Written as sheet music it is just six notes. Same sound, far fewer things to read.
cap.2: Changing basis re-describes the same vector in new coordinates. Pick waves (sines and cosines) as the coordinates, and a periodic signal needs only a few of them.
cap.3: An orthonormal change of basis is a rotation: nothing is lost and lengths are kept, but a signal built from a few frequencies has only a few non-zero coordinates.

cap.1: Numbers on a 113-hour clock go round and round, and adding is just turning the hand. Waves that fit the clock exactly are the natural way to describe turning.
cap.2: For each whole number k, cos(2πkx/113) and sin(2πkx/113) repeat exactly once per lap of the clock. Adding x and y adds their angles, which waves handle neatly.
cap.3: With w_k = 2πk/p, angle-addition identities turn products of waves in x and y into waves in x + y, which is why the trained model's algorithm is written in this basis.

chapters.name: The wave dictionary
chapters.title: the 1D Fourier basis for p = 5 (before normalising)

cap.1: Build a dictionary of waves: a flat line, then a cosine and a sine for each speed. For a 5-hour clock that is five waves, one per row.
cap.2: make_fourier_basis(p): a constant row plus cos and sin rows for k = 1 to (p-1)/2, each normalised to length 1. For p = 113 that is 1 + 2×56 = 113 rows.
cap.3: The rows are orthonormal, so F @ W_E expresses every embedding column in the Fourier basis and F.T undoes it. Check it: F @ F.T should be the identity.

chapters.name: Six bright notes
chapters.note: schematic heights; frequencies from ARENA's checkpoint

cap.1: Rewrite the number table in waves and the static clears: almost every wave is silent, and about six ring out loud. The model picked six notes.
cap.2: Compute fourier_basis @ W_E (number rows only, not '='), take each row's norm and plot by frequency. Only a handful are non-trivial: 14, 31, 35, 41, 42, 52 in ARENA's checkpoint.
cap.3: W_E has non-trivial norm only at the key frequencies; neurons then cluster by frequency, and W_logit projects only onto cos and sin of those same frequencies.

chapters.name: The off-by-one
chapters.verdict: Nothing screams when a frequency index is off by one. Check it by projection.

cap.1: Count the notes from zero instead of one and every note comes out one step low. It still looks musical, so nothing warns you. Check by playing it back.
cap.2: The 2D basis helper starts at k = 1: slice 0 of arrange_by_2d_freqs is frequency 1. Argmax gives indices; add one before calling them frequencies.
cap.3: Verify rather than trust: reconstruct cos(w_k(x+y)) at each claimed key frequency and project the logits onto it. A wrong frequency projects to near nothing.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Find the reading where weights go quiet
Sparse is what makes weights readable
Next: progress measures from the mechanism

cap.1: The trick is general: view the same numbers in a new language until most go quiet. What remains is what the model really does: step one to steering it.
cap.2: Reading the weights in the basis where they are sparse is how the grokking algorithm was decoded, and it is what lets progress measures track the circuit rather than the loss.
cap.3: Periodic in the standard basis means sparse in the Fourier basis. When no symmetry hands you the basis, interpretability learns a sparse dictionary instead (sparse autoencoders).

coda.title: Find the notes in a mystery row

readouts.label: non-zero entries: samples vs frequencies
readouts.f: range(113).filter(x => abs(Math.cos(2*PI*14*x/113) + b*Math.sin(2*PI*31*x/113)) > 0.01).length + ' of 113 samples vs ' + (b > 0 ? '2 frequencies' : '1 frequency')

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: sqrt(pow(2/113*sum(range(113).map(x => (Math.cos(2*PI*14*x/113) + b*Math.sin(2*PI*31*x/113))*Math.cos(2*PI*k*x/113))), 2) + pow(2/113*sum(range(113).map(x => (Math.cos(2*PI*14*x/113) + b*Math.sin(2*PI*31*x/113))*Math.sin(2*PI*k*x/113))), 2)) > 0.1 ? 'a note rings at k = ' + k : 'silent: this wave is orthogonal to the row'

caption.1: The blue row looks like noise. Slide the probe through every speed and watch the strength: zero almost everywhere, ringing at just two speeds.
caption.2: Strength is the length of the row's projection onto cos(k) and sin(k). Orthogonality makes every wrong k exactly zero, so a dense row of 113 numbers becomes two notes.
caption.3: Coefficient = (2/p)·Σx s(x)·cos(w_k x), likewise for sin; the pair's norm per k is, up to scaling, the per-frequency norm you plot for W_E.

where_else: JPEG: images go sparse in a cosine basis, so most coefficients can be dropped
Sinusoidal positional embeddings: positions written as waves at many speeds
Sparse autoencoders: when no symmetry hands you the basis, learn a sparse dictionary
Music: spectrum analysers and equalisers show sound by frequency

hamming.what: Re-expressing a weight matrix in a basis of sines and cosines over the input, so periodic structure shows up as a few large coefficients.
hamming.when: When the inputs are cyclic, like numbers mod p, and the weights look dense and random in the standard basis.
hamming.why: Periodic in the standard basis means sparse in the Fourier basis, and sparse is what makes a model's algorithm readable.

object.title: The two-way table
object.subtitle: One small number table, read two ways: busy bars in the standard reading, one quiet lit pair in the wave reading.

cap.1: A toy number table on an 11-hour clock, read number by number: every bar is busy.
cap.2: Rows are the inputs x = 0..10, columns are embedding dimensions. Dense: nothing stands out.
cap.3: Standard basis: each column is a sampled wave cos(w_3 x + φ_c), so nearly every entry is non-zero.

cap.1: Same table, read in waves. Everything goes quiet except two rows: the cosine and sine of one speed.
cap.2: In the Fourier basis only cos 3 and sin 3 are non-zero, in every column. Dense became sparse.
cap.3: Rows 2k-1 and 2k hold cos and sin of frequency k; bar heights are coefficient sizes, scaled.

cap.1: Change which speed the table uses and the lit pair moves, but it is always a pair.
cap.2: A shifted wave needs both cos and sin at its frequency, so each frequency lights two rows.
cap.3: cos(wx + φ) = cos φ·cos(wx) − sin φ·sin(wx): a phase is a mix of the cos and sin rows.

cap.1: Back in the number-by-number reading, the new table looks just as noisy. The reading changed, not the data.
cap.2: Same numbers, rotated. The change of basis loses nothing; it only changes what is easy to read.
cap.3: An orthonormal rotation preserves norms: the total squared height matches in both readings (before scaling).

cap.1: That is the whole trick: find the reading where the weights go quiet.
cap.2: For the grokking model that reading shows about six key frequencies; the rest is near zero.
cap.3: Sparsity in the right basis is what made the algorithm readable, and what the progress measures build on.

predict.q: Your key frequencies come out as 13, 30, 34, 40, 41, 51. What went wrong?

options.t: Off by one: slice 0 of the helper is frequency 1

predict.why: The 2D helper indexes from k = 1, so argmax indices are one below the true frequencies. Add one, then verify by projection.

predict.q: Does switching to the Fourier basis change what the model computes?

options.t: No: it is a rotation, the same numbers re-described
Yes: it filters out the noise

predict.why: An orthonormal change of basis loses nothing. Deleting directions afterwards is a separate step, an ablation.

predict.q: Why does a cos-and-sin pair light up for each frequency?

options.t: A shifted wave is a mix of cos and sin at that frequency
Each frequency is counted twice by mistake

predict.why: cos(wx + φ) = cos φ·cos(wx) − sin φ·sin(wx).

object.where: Anything periodic: sound spectra, JPEG's cosine blocks, sinusoidal positional encodings.
